title: SYSK Selects: How Bonsai Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (chosen by Chuck, originally recorded May 2016) on bonsai: its meaning and history from Tang dynasty China (penjing) to Japan, the Kamakura-era appreciation of deformed trees, the Edo-era isolation and Western exposure through 1878 Paris and 1909 London exhibitions. The hosts cover formal and informal upright, slanting, semi-cascade and cascade, literati, broom, landscape, root-over-rock and multi-trunk styles; which plants can be used (juniper as a beginner choice); starting a bonsai (buying, root trimming, potting, wiring, soil, placement, watering, fertilizing); advanced techniques like deadwood (jin, shari) and sabamiki; notable old trees such as the National Bonsai and Penjing Museum white pine; and a Lost in Translation tangent. The episode also includes a listener email about skyscraper wind design after the tornado episode.

segments.title: Intro and listener tangents
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Selects episode on bonsai, recorded May 2016. The hosts banter about listener complaints over tangents, a sponsor mention of a Chicago liqueur, and the spelling and pronunciation of bonsai.

segments.title: What bonsai is and its critics
segments.summary: Bonsai is described as a plant in a tiny container, distinct from fake toy trees. The hosts discuss criticism that it bends nature to human will, and frame bonsai as living sculpture.

segments.title: History of bonsai from China to Japan
segments.summary: Origins in China as penjing, with tomb paintings from the Tang dynasty and a legend of a Qin-era emperor. The art moved to Japan, where a Kamakura-period scroll praised loving deformity, and it spread from monks to elites to common people.

segments.title: Japan's isolation and Western exposure
segments.summary: Japan's seventeenth-century isolation policy and its later opening under American pressure led by Matthew Perry. Bonsai reached Western audiences at the Paris 1878 and London 1909 exhibitions.

segments.title: Sponsor break and Cracked tangent
segments.summary: Brief discussion of Cracked magazine's revival, plus a break.

segments.title: Formal and informal upright styles
segments.summary: The hosts describe the chokkan formal upright style with a tapering trunk for forced perspective, and the moyogi informal upright style that bends and twists.

segments.title: Slanting, cascade and literati styles
segments.summary: Slanting style with a leaning trunk and parallel branches, cascade and semi-cascade styles that hang over the pot edge, and the literati style viewed from below. The hosts note the importance of pot and plant harmony and the front and back of a bonsai.

segments.title: Broom, landscape, root-over-rock and multi-trunk styles
segments.summary: Broom style resembles an idealized oak or maple. Landscape style recreates a miniature scene, and root-over-rock trains roots to cling to stone. Multi-trunk (forest) style gives the look of several trees from one root system. Notable old trees are mentioned, including a nearly 400-year-old white pine at the National Bonsai and Penjing Museum.

segments.title: Choosing plants for bonsai
segments.summary: Bonsai is about dwarfing ordinary trees by container and root trimming, not special miniature species. Most bonsai are outdoor plants, though some indoor varieties exist. Junipers are suggested as a good beginner plant, and small-leaved, dense trees are preferred.

segments.title: Starting a bonsai: buying, roots, potting, wiring
segments.summary: Buying a nursery plant, trimming roughly two-thirds of the roots, choosing a pot with drainage, gravel, and soil mix, and using wire to shape branches without cutting into the trunk. The hosts also cover the first watering by submersion and acclimating the plant to sun.

segments.title: Branch placement, watering, fertilizing and advanced techniques
segments.summary: Branches are placed in alternating positions at about one-third intervals for balance. Care includes rotating for sun, pest control, daily watering, weekly fertilizing, and repotting every couple of years. Advanced deadwood techniques are discussed: jin, shari, and sabamiki.

segments.title: Lost in Translation tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film Lost in Translation, its bonsai-related scene, and Sofia Coppola's other films.

segments.title: Listener mail on skyscraper wind design
segments.summary: A listener who is a civil engineer writes about why skyscrapers are not perfect cylinders, since wind hits a cylinder as a single wall of force. The hosts thank the listener.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact details and sign off.
